Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

detfield 0.1.1

First release.

Range tests and detection models

  • range_test_counts() counts a range test from its files (detections, receivers, and range-test tags with positions and delays) into hourly sent and heard per receiver and tag. Hours in which a receiver heard nothing from a tag are kept with heard = 0, because a curve fitted to the heard hours alone reaches too far.
  • de_logistic() builds a detection curve from d50 and d05, the distances at which half and 5% of transmissions are heard, at one depth or interpolated between depths. It refuses d05 <= d50. Its print gives the distances to four significant digits.
  • de_model() builds a detection model from a fitted glm or glmmTMB model, a table of curve values, a function or a de_logistic() curve. The spread of one receiver’s hourly detection probability about the curve, sigma$station_hour, is carried as given and never fitted. A non-NA sigma$station_day stops. Covariates that change by day, such as wind, enter as modulators.
  • de_model() warns when it is given a glmmTMB fit whose formula holds a smooth (s(), te(), t2() or ti()) and no re.form: glmmTMB fits the wiggly part of a smooth as a random effect, so with the default re.form = NA the smooth reaches the field as a straight line. The warning names the term and the two ways out: fit the smooth in mgcv, or pass re.form = NULL.
  • de_model() predicts a bam(discrete = TRUE) fit with discrete = FALSE, so each pair is predicted on its own. A discrete prediction discretises all the rows it is given together, which moves a pair’s detection probability with the other pairs of the field: by up to 0.12 logit on the range-model article’s model (https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/06_discrete_prediction.R).
  • de_model(blocked = ) sets a logit offset for receiver-cell pairs whose line of sight crosses land. The default, 0, reads the curve at the distance through water.

Detection fields

  • water_distances() measures the distance through water from every receiver to every water cell, going round land, and records whether the straight line stays in water. A receiver just on land snaps to the centre of the nearest water cell, by at most one and a half cell diagonals, and the warning gives each move in metres. A grid with no land cells, no CRS or no water, and a serial found at two positions, stop or warn with a plain message.
  • water_distances() reads the grid’s units as metres on the ground. It refuses a grid in longitude and latitude, in a unit other than the metre, or in a CRS whose scale at the raster centre differs from 1 by more than 1 percent on its two axes or its diagonals. The scale is measured on four 1 km segments, and the refusal names it and the UTM zone of the centre. The Stoney example grid in Web Mercator has a scale of about 1.40 there and is refused. A CRS whose scale cannot be measured, such as a local engineering CRS, is refused too.
  • The land test of water_distances() decides a line that passes within a thousandth of a cell side of a cell corner at the corner, whichever side it passes: grazing one land cell’s corner leaves the line clear, and passing where two land cells meet diagonally blocks it. A station a few millimetres off its cell centre, as a station file with latitude and longitude to seven decimals gives, has the lines of sight of one at the centre.
  • Where land lies on the straight line, water_distances() gives the exact shortest path through water: straight legs that bend only at the corners where water turns round land, found by Dijkstra’s algorithm over those corners with the land test as line of sight. The exact path starts at the receiver itself, so a receiver moved by millimetres moves distance_m by millimetres.
  • control = list(path = "grid") keeps the straight line where it stays in water and, where land lies on it, takes the path between cell centres in steps to the eight neighbouring cells, by terra::gridDist(). On the 70 receivers of stoney_track it gives the straight line on all 92,798 clear pairs. On the 244,392 blocked pairs it gives 0.664 to 1.164 times the exact path, 1.059 on average, and it reaches the 70 pairs of the one cell the exact path counts as unreachable (https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/05_grid_path.R). positionR 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 took the 8-neighbour grid path for every pair; from 1.2.0 the straight line is used where no land crosses it. On open water the 8-neighbour path is up to 8.2% longer than the straight line, 5.5% on average over the 92,728 clear pairs off the receiver’s own cell.
  • On the 70 receivers of stoney_track, water_distances() takes 3.9 s on one core and the grid option 1.3 s. Over the same lake split into 25 m cells it takes 88 s and 28 s. These are medians of 5 and 3 runs on one machine (https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/04_memory_time.R).
  • Two water cells that touch only where two land cells meet diagonally are not joined, since the land test closes that point; water reached only through such a point is counted in the unreachable attribute. One Stoney cell is cut off this way. A receiver within the corner tolerance of such a point is tested on the cells ahead of it.
  • The land test is one geometric rule for every leg: a segment is blocked when it comes deeper than a thousandth of a cell side into land, or that close to a closed gap it does not start in. A receiver within 10 cm of a grid line is blocked by land lying on both sides of that line, and a receiver just outside the tolerance of a closed gap sees its own cell. positionR from 1.2.0 tested 50 points along each line whatever its length, which misses land narrower than the gap between points.
  • de_field() gives every water cell a detection probability for every receiver, read at the distance through water and the receiver’s depth, and counts in a message the pairs with land on the line of sight.
  • system_de() gives, per day, the probability that at least k listening receivers detect a transmission from each cell. It accepts the listening table that detqc::as_detfield_input() returns. A day on which every receiver is "off" or "deaf" gives 0 in every cell. A day with no listening receiver for any other reason, such as "not_downloaded", is left out, because its receivers may have listened with their data missing. On a day with some listening receivers, the coverage comes from those receivers. A receiver the field does not hold is an error on any row of listening, listening or not.
  • system_de(transmissions = ) gives the same probability for a bin in which the tag sent that many transmissions: the probability that the bin is detected from each cell. The default, 1, gives the per-transmission result unchanged.

Location surfaces

  • bin_detections() counts each animal’s detections per hour (or day) at every listening receiver, silent receivers included, and the transmissions the tag sent from its delay. It reads listening as receiver-days, deployments or both; a receiver listens in a bin when its deployment covers at least min_cover of it. Animals with two or more codes need codes = "shared" or "independent". The attribute rate_check flags animals whose transmission count looks doubled or halved.
  • location_surface() turns each animal’s counts in a bin into the probability that it was in each water cell. likelihood = "binomial", the default, uses detections and misses at every listening receiver; "presence_only" uses the detections alone, as a check when the curve’s level is not trusted. With overdispersion = "station_hour" the spread is integrated by Gauss-Hermite quadrature. The bin table gives a misfit test per bin (misfit_p), the distance from the most probable cell to the detecting receivers (mode_dist_m) and the probability near the receiver with the most detections (near_mass).
  • A run of location_surface() in which every bin is degenerate stops with an error of class detfield_error_degenerate; a stop on one bin has class detfield_error_degenerate_bin. Both also have class detfield_error, so a caller can catch them by class.
  • credible_region() gives the smallest set of cells holding a level of each bin’s probability, with its area, as a table or a raster. sample_locations() draws cells in proportion to their probability; its attribute estimand says that the draws describe detected bins only.
  • The print of a surface counts bins with misfit, bins with almost no probability near the receiver that heard the animal most, and the distance of the modes from the detecting receivers. The radius of the near count is, per receiver, the distance to the farthest cell centre at which the field gives a detection probability of 0.5 or more.

Used and available points

  • sample_available() draws availability points for each animal, detected bin and presence draw from the whole detection surface of the bin’s date: in proportion to the probability that the bin is detected from each cell (system_de(transmissions = )), or uniformly over the cells at or above a probability (uniform_above). positionR 1.x drew availability from the same surface but weighted by the per-transmission probability, kept cells strictly above a minimum of 0.001 and below an optional maximum, and drew one set per fish and time period. Here the weight is the coverage table given, with no minimum or maximum, the uniform mode keeps cells at or above the threshold, and each presence draw gets its own set, for multiple imputation. Pass the hourly table: an hour is a presence when the animal was heard at least once in it. With the per-transmission weight, simulated animals with no preference showed one (-0.091 per m of bottom depth on their true tracks, 95% CI -0.161 to -0.020). Strata with no cell to draw are dropped, counted in a warning and listed in the attribute dropped.
  • used_available() stacks the used and available points into one table for a conditional logistic regression: one stratum per animal, bin and draw with its used point (case = 1) and its available points (case = 0), and one column per covariate layer read at each point’s cell. Rows with a missing covariate are dropped and counted by reason in the attribute dropped. It fits no model.

Figures

  • plot() of a detection model draws the curves from 0 m to the distance where the last curve falls below 0.01.
  • plot() of a detection field maps one receiver, or the probability that any receiver detects a transmission, on the magma scale, with receivers as yellow rings and the scale bar at the bottom right.
  • plot() of a location surface maps one animal and bin with the outlines of its 50% and 95% credible regions and the receivers listening in the bin, drawn by layer_receivers(), on a map at least 1.5 km across. Only receivers inside the map are drawn and keyed. The colour runs from 0 to the bin’s largest cell probability, which is the top label of the key. The title gives the animal and bin on one line.
  • layer_receivers() draws receivers on a map as rings over a dark ring: yellow for a receiver that heard the animal, sized by its count when a count column is given, and white for a listening receiver that heard none.
  • theme_positionr(), scale_fill_depth(), scale_fill_probability() and annotation_scale_bar() draw every figure of the positionR packages in one style. scale_fill_depth() reads depth stored as positive or negative metres.

Example data

  • stoney_track: five simulated animals in Stoney Lake, Ontario, for 48 hours from 1 June 2024, with 70 receivers on a grid, every transmission heard or missed, and the true tracks. The array is dense enough that most detected hours are heard by two or more receivers.
  • stoney_selection: forty simulated animals on the same 70 receivers with a known preference for bottom depth (twenty for shallow water, twenty with none), their true tracks, the position draws of every detected hour, the coverage of the array per day, and the per-animal results and hourly depths of a trial over five preferences, two arrays and two blocks of animals.
  • stoney_range_test: a range test at receiver depths of 1 m and 25 m, counted by range_test_counts() from the files included in inst/extdata.
  • stoney_range_covariates: a range test with two tag models, two depths and daily wind.
  • The Stoney Lake depth raster and the study’s deployments, detections and tags are included as files, so every example reads the same inputs a user’s own study gives.

Articles

  • “Habitat selection: depth use from hourly positions” sets the depth of position draws against the true depth of 40 simulated animals, then draws availability points and reports a trial of the depth coefficient from positions against the true track. “Hourly positions against the true track” links to it for depth use.
  • The articles are “Range models: bring your own, or start from two distances”, “Hourly positions against the true track”, “Habitat selection: depth use from hourly positions” and “Position fish from a cleaned detection set”.
  • The walk through the package’s steps is the Get started vignette, vignette("detfield"); the home page holds one example. “Position fish from a cleaned detection set” is on the website only, as it needs detqc installed.
